weeks.title: ENGINEERING SOFTWARE THAT PEOPLE CAN DEPEND ON
weeks.question: What makes working code an engineered system?
outcomes: Distinguish a locally correct function from a dependable user-facing service.
Identify stakeholders, system boundaries, and competing quality concerns.
Explain why delivery and maintenance belong in the engineering lifecycle.
Separate an observation, an assumption, and evidence supporting a claim.
Explain one technical decision in terms of benefit, cost, and affected people.

checks.question: What is wrong with two successful overlapping confirmations?
checks.answer: They violate the intended exclusivity rule even when each screen and request appears successful.

checks.question: Why include support staff in the stakeholder map?
checks.answer: Their diagnostic needs influence observability, documentation, privacy, and recovery decisions.

checks.question: Does passing one booking example establish correctness for simultaneous requests?
checks.answer: No. The evidence does not cover that interaction condition.

checks.question: Which representation answers “What happens after a timeout?”
checks.answer: A state model or a sequence/timeline view, depending on whether the question concerns possible states or a particular interaction.

scenes.instructor_title: Two green confirmations cannot both be right
scenes.visual_idea: Two browser cards beside one shared room calendar. Three controlled beats reveal request, stored state, and user consequence.
scenes.situation: Situation and prediction: Ari and Bo each see “Confirmed” for C101 at 10:00. Ask, “What evidence would let us decide whether the system worked?” Reveal the calendar containing two overlapping confirmed bookings, then the people arriving at the same door. Show that an attractive interface and a successful response are not the whole behavior.
scenes.changed_condition: Change only the confirmation rule: a shared decision now admits one request and rejects the conflicting one. Compare inconvenience from an honest rejection with harm from a false promise. Do not explain transactions yet; preserve that question for later.
scenes.principle: Engineering judges behavior against an intended outcome and its consequences, not appearance alone.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the two-confirmation outcome and the one-confirmation outcome, with the violated rule written below both.

scenes.instructor_title: The booking button is not the whole system
scenes.visual_idea: A context map with the service inside a boundary and users, campus identity, room records, and notification delivery outside.
scenes.situation: Ask which parts the team can change directly. Reveal one interaction at a time and label arrows with their meaning. A student request, an identity assertion, and a notification are not interchangeable kinds of information.
scenes.changed_condition: Make the notification provider unavailable without changing room storage. Ask which user outcomes remain possible. Keep the boundary fixed so the class sees a dependency rather than a new diagram.
scenes.principle: A system boundary identifies responsibility and dependencies; it does not make external behavior disappear.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Use one labeled context map with the unavailable dependency marked by both text and a broken-line symbol.

scenes.instructor_title: The same screen can serve one person and exclude another
scenes.visual_idea: A stakeholder map connected to concrete concerns; an accessible keyboard path sits beside the visual interface.
scenes.situation: Ask who is affected besides the person clicking Reserve. Reveal a student needing step-free access, room staff handling closures, support staff diagnosing mistakes, and a maintainer interpreting old decisions. Translate each concern into a question the system must answer.
scenes.changed_condition: Change the user interaction from mouse to keyboard. The visually polished version initially has no reachable confirmation control; the corrected version does. Compare task completion, not the attractiveness of the two screens. Introduce accessibility as part of whether the service works. [S25]
scenes.principle: Quality depends on the people and conditions included in the definition of success.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the stakeholder-concern table and the successful keyboard route; describe the failed route in text.

scenes.instructor_title: Faster is not a complete description of better
scenes.visual_idea: A comparison table with response time, correctness, recoverability, privacy, and change effort; avoid an unexplained radar chart.
scenes.situation: Offer two fictional designs: immediate confirmation from an unchecked local view, and confirmation after an authoritative availability decision. Ask which is better before revealing their behavior. Separate quality attributes from optional features.
scenes.changed_condition: Keep correctness mandatory and change the response-time target. Discuss which optimizations preserve the rule and which merely hide a delay. Clearly label illustrative measurements and never imply that accuracy must always be traded for speed.
scenes.principle: Compare alternatives under stated constraints; some requirements are conditions of acceptance rather than points in a score.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the alternatives, assumptions, and a short rationale rather than a winner badge.

scenes.instructor_title: A failure can teach the next requirement
scenes.visual_idea: A loop connecting need, model, implementation, checks, release, operation, and revision; an incident card travels through it.
scenes.situation: Predict where a missing “notification failed” behavior would be discovered. Reveal that it may emerge during a requirements conversation, an integration check, or operation. Follow the incident back to an updated user message and a new verification check.
scenes.changed_condition: Move the first useful feedback earlier while keeping the defect the same. Compare the kinds of rework involved, without presenting an invented universal cost-of-defect multiplier. Explain iteration as revisiting understanding and increment as adding usable capability.
scenes.principle: The lifecycle is a network of feedback loops, not a one-way conveyor ending when code runs.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the full loop and two annotated feedback paths, including what information changed.

scenes.instructor_title: What would make us believe this works?
scenes.visual_idea: Three columns labeled Claim, Check, and Remaining uncertainty; cards move only when a reason is supplied.
scenes.situation: Present “It looks right,” “It passed one example,” and “It met the stated checks under these conditions.” Ask which evidence supports which claim. Reveal a counterexample outside the tested conditions without implying that all prior testing was worthless.
scenes.changed_condition: Change the workload from one user to simultaneous users. Compare the unchanged claim with the newly exposed assumption. Introduce the course habit of stating both evidence and its limits.
scenes.principle: A check supports a bounded claim; confidence without scope is difficult to evaluate.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the completed claim-check-uncertainty table, retaining the counterexample.

scenes.instructor_title: Who carries the cost of an engineering shortcut?
scenes.visual_idea: A consequence map linking a decision to users, support effort, data exposure, and future change.
scenes.situation: Show a support log containing more personal information than needed to diagnose a failure. Ask who benefits and who takes the risk. Reveal an alternative containing a request identifier and failure category instead of private booking details.
scenes.changed_condition: Change the support question so that one additional field is genuinely needed. Compare deliberate, justified collection with collecting everything by default. Keep this an engineering discussion, not jurisdiction-specific legal advice.
scenes.principle: Professional responsibility includes the consequences imposed on people who did not make the technical choice.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the minimal diagnostic record and the rationale for each retained field.

scenes.instructor_title: One domain, many kinds of explanation
scenes.visual_idea: A course map that changes representation: requirement card, state diagram, dependency graph, test table, release path, and incident timeline.
scenes.situation: Ask whether one flowchart could explain all of these questions equally well. Reveal each representation with a single example of the question it answers. Introduce the recurring Campus Rooms case without exposing authoring tools.
scenes.changed_condition: Keep the booking behavior fixed and switch from “Who depends on this?” to “What happened first?” Compare the dependency graph with the sequence diagram. Then change the actor: the same booking change is drafted by an automated assistant instead of a colleague. Ask which representations and checks are no longer needed. None; that is the through-line the course returns to in Week 13.
scenes.principle: Choose a representation for the question, not a diagram style for the whole course.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the course map as a question-to-representation reference, including the row for a change drafted by an automated assistant.

weeks.title: FROM AMBIGUOUS REQUESTS TO VERIFIABLE REQUIREMENTS
weeks.question: How would we know that a requirement has been satisfied?
outcomes: Identify ambiguity, missing stakeholders, and hidden assumptions in a request.
Turn a request into observable behavior with boundary and failure cases.
Distinguish a requirement from a solution decision and a supporting assumption.
Connect a requirement to a design decision and an independent verification check.
Explain how a changed requirement affects linked evidence.

checks.question: Is “Use Framework X to make booking fast” a clear behavior requirement?
checks.answer: It mixes a solution choice with an underspecified quality objective; define the needed outcome and conditions separately.

checks.question: Should a 120-minute booking satisfy R-02?
checks.answer: Yes. The upper limit is inclusive; other validity and availability checks still apply.

checks.question: What is missing from “Search must finish in 500 milliseconds”?
checks.answer: At least the measurement boundary, workload, proportion or percentile, and conditions.

checks.question: What does selecting R-03 in the matrix tell us?
checks.answer: Which decisions and checks are linked to cancellation authorization; those links need review when the rule changes.

scenes.instructor_title: One sentence, three incompatible interpretations
scenes.visual_idea: An editable-looking request card branches into three concrete screen outcomes; no actual language-model call is involved.
scenes.situation: Ask students to predict the behavior implied by “Make booking fair.” Reveal first-come access, per-user limits, and staff-priority interpretations. Show that all three could be defended from the same sentence. Add questions about who decides, what is scarce, and what outcome matters.
scenes.changed_condition: Change only the stakeholder answering the question. Compare the resulting rules and surface the conflict rather than silently selecting one. Settle this lecture's scope on exclusive booking of available rooms; fairness policy remains an explicit open decision.
scenes.principle: Ambiguity is resolved through examples and stakeholder decisions, not through more confident wording.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the ambiguous sentence, the competing interpretations, and the clarified scope.

scenes.instructor_title: An omitted user can hide an entire requirement
scenes.visual_idea: A context map gains questions at its boundaries; facts, assumptions, and open decisions have different labels and shapes.
scenes.situation: Ask what must be learned before accepting a request from a guest. Reveal questions about identity, cancellation rights, accessibility, and room closures. [S25] Separate something a stakeholder stated from something a developer inferred.
scenes.changed_condition: Introduce an external visitor as a new stakeholder but keep this release's campus-member boundary. Compare explicitly deferred behavior with an accidental omission.
scenes.principle: An explicit boundary and an open-question register make uncertainty discussable.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the scope boundary and a compact fact-assumption-question table.

scenes.instructor_title: Turn “short booking” into a rule we can examine
scenes.visual_idea: A duration ruler, a requirement card, and example outcomes update together.
scenes.situation: Show 29, 30, 120, and 121 minute requests. Ask which should be accepted before revealing R-02: durations are at least 30 and at most 120 minutes, inclusive. Explain actor, condition, expected behavior, and rejection behavior. Keep the rule separate from a proposed slider widget.
scenes.changed_condition: Change only the upper limit from 120 to 90 minutes in a clearly labeled temporary variant. Compare the affected examples and restore the canonical 120-minute rule afterward. Include an invalid end-before-start request to show that one boundary rule does not describe every validity condition. Then add the AI beat: two prepared, synthetic drafting requests go to an automated assistant, one carrying the sentence “keep bookings short” and one carrying R-02. Show the two candidate rules side by side: the first invents a limit, the second implements 30 through 120 inclusive. No live model call; the candidates are authored fixtures.
scenes.principle: A useful requirement makes meaningful differences between acceptable and unacceptable outcomes visible.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the canonical rule and an input-expected-outcome table; label the 90-minute variant as a comparison only. Print the two candidate rules with the request that produced each.

scenes.instructor_title: “Fast” needs a workload and a measurement boundary
scenes.visual_idea: A response-time distribution appears beside workload and measurement-condition cards.
scenes.situation: Ask whether a 200 millisecond response proves the system is fast. Reveal Q-01: in the specified teaching fixture, the 95th percentile of search API response time should not exceed 500 milliseconds under 50 concurrent users. Explain that this is an authored target, not a universal service standard.
scenes.changed_condition: Change the workload while holding the target and code constant. Compare what was measured with what was claimed. Distinguish service-boundary response time from the student's whole browser experience.
scenes.principle: A quality requirement needs a quantity, a boundary, conditions, and an acceptance rule.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the distribution, the explicit target, the fixture assumptions, and the measurement boundary.

scenes.instructor_title: A precise requirement can still describe the wrong thing
scenes.visual_idea: A three-part strip: stakeholder need, precise statement, and observed behavior.
scenes.situation: Show a system that perfectly enforces a 30-minute maximum because someone transcribed the desired 120-minute maximum incorrectly. Ask whether implementation checks against the written statement would catch the misunderstanding. Reveal the original stakeholder example.
scenes.changed_condition: Keep the implementation unchanged and correct the intended requirement. Compare verification against a specification with validation of the intended need, acknowledging that actual practices can overlap.
scenes.principle: We must question both whether the system matches its description and whether the description matches the need.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the two questions and the mismatch connecting them.

scenes.instructor_title: A requirement should lead somewhere
scenes.visual_idea: A small matrix links requirement IDs to design decisions, examples, and checks. Selecting a cell highlights its evidence chain.
scenes.situation: Begin with R-01 and a blank matrix. Ask what evidence should connect “no overlapping confirmations” to an implementation. Reveal an authoritative conflict decision, boundary examples, and a concurrent-request check. Add R-03 with an ownership decision and an authorization check. Explain why a matrix suits coverage better than a moving pipeline.
scenes.changed_condition: Change R-03 so a delegated staff role may cancel under a recorded reason. Highlight only the decisions and checks that genuinely depend on that rule. Leave unrelated duration tests unchanged and mark the new policy as a variant requiring a stakeholder decision.
scenes.principle: Traceability makes relationships inspectable; a link is useful only when its meaning and evidence are current.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the readable matrix, a legend, and the change-impact highlight with text labels.

scenes.instructor_title: The loudest request is not automatically the next one
scenes.visual_idea: A decision table compares user benefit, dependency, uncertainty, consequence, and effort range.
scenes.situation: Offer three requests: correct duplicate confirmations, add decorative room photos, and make cancellation accessible. Ask what information is needed to prioritize them. Reveal consequences and dependencies without hiding judgments inside a mysterious score.
scenes.changed_condition: Change one condition: a room closure is scheduled tomorrow in the fictional scenario. Compare how urgency and risk influence order without rewriting the underlying value of the requests.
scenes.principle: Priority is a reasoned choice under constraints, not a permanent property of a feature.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the decision table and the rationale for the selected order.

scenes.instructor_title: A changed rule should not leave old evidence pretending to be current
scenes.visual_idea: A versioned requirement card is connected to a change note, an owner, and stale/current evidence badges.
scenes.situation: Ask what must happen when a duration rule changes after tests have been written. Reveal the changed statement, its rationale, the linked examples requiring revision, and a clearly dated decision. Retain prior wording as history rather than making it disappear.
scenes.changed_condition: Change the request from a rule update to a wording correction that preserves behavior. Compare semantic change with editorial change and avoid triggering the same response mechanically.
scenes.principle: Manage the meaning of a change, its rationale, and its evidence together.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the before-and-after requirement and the explicit affected/unaffected list.

weeks.title: MODELING BEHAVIOR, DATA, AND USER INTERACTION
weeks.question: Which model answers the question we are actually asking?
outcomes: Choose a model suited to a behavior, structure, or interaction question.
Read a state transition with an event, condition, and outcome.
Distinguish a stored booking from a transient interface or request state.
Explain entity identity and relationships without duplicating shared facts.
Locate a contradiction between a requirement, a diagram, and an interface message.

checks.question: A response times out after persistence. Is the booking necessarily absent?
checks.answer: No. The requester may not know the result even though the booking exists.

checks.question: Why reference a room ID instead of copying its current name everywhere?
checks.answer: Identity remains stable when the displayed name changes; historical snapshots should be modeled deliberately.

checks.question: Which model best exposes combinations of ownership and status?
checks.answer: A decision table.

checks.question: How can a diagram be tested before code exists?
checks.answer: Walk concrete examples through it and compare outcomes with requirements and complementary models.

scenes.instructor_title: Follow the person before drawing the internals
scenes.visual_idea: A user journey strip with goal, action, visible feedback, and uncertainty at each step.
scenes.situation: Ask what a student needs to know after pressing Reserve. Reveal the difference between “request sent,” “booking confirmed,” and “could not determine the result.” Follow one ordinary request before adding technical actors.
scenes.changed_condition: Remove the confirmation message but retain a successful stored booking. Compare system state with user understanding and discuss the resulting duplicate-click risk.
scenes.principle: A user journey exposes information needs that an internal component diagram can miss.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the journey with the visible message and underlying state on separate rows.

scenes.instructor_title: A booking cannot be in every state at once
scenes.visual_idea: Two deliberately separate state models: request/UI states above, stored booking states below. A current-state marker moves only on valid events.
scenes.situation: Start in Draft and ask what Submit means. Reveal Submitting, then Confirmed, Rejected, or Unknown outcome when a response is lost. Link confirmed results to a stored booking record. In the stored model, a permitted cancellation changes Confirmed to Cancelled. Label events and conditions before discussing terminology.
scenes.changed_condition: Change the current state to Cancelled and replay Cancel. Compare a stable, clearly defined repeated response with an accidental second state change. Ask which transitions are intentionally absent. Keep UI timeout separate from deletion of the stored booking.
scenes.principle: State models clarify which changes are possible, what triggers them, and which facts are actually known.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print both models with a legend and a short example explaining why a timeout is not proof of failure.

scenes.instructor_title: Two copies of a room name can disagree
scenes.visual_idea: Entity cards for User, Room, and Booking; relationship lines highlight identity and cardinality.
scenes.situation: Show two booking records containing copied room capacity values. Ask what happens when the room capacity changes. Reveal a Room entity with a stable identifier and bookings referencing it. Explain that a booking belongs to one user and one room, while each user or room can be associated with many bookings over time.
scenes.changed_condition: Change a room's display name while keeping its identifier. Compare stable references with matching on a mutable name. Also show a deliberately preserved historical snapshot and explain that duplication may be intentional when the meaning is historical rather than current.
scenes.principle: Model identity and the meaning of a fact before deciding where to store it.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the relationship diagram and current-fact versus historical-snapshot comparison.

scenes.instructor_title: Some rules are clearer as rows than as arrows
scenes.visual_idea: A decision table combines membership, ownership, booking state, and start time for cancellation.
scenes.situation: Ask whether an authenticated campus member may cancel every booking. Reveal R-03: a requester may cancel their own future confirmed booking. Fill representative allowed and denied rows, then expose a missing past-booking row.
scenes.changed_condition: Change only ownership while holding authentication true. Compare the decision and point to the exact rule responsible. Avoid inventing a universal staff override.
scenes.principle: A decision table makes combinations and missing cases easier to inspect.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print all core rows, the rule, and a note identifying the policy boundary.

scenes.instructor_title: The same final state can hide different interaction histories
scenes.visual_idea: A sequence diagram with browser, booking service, authoritative store, and notification worker.
scenes.situation: Ask what must happen before a true confirmation can be shown. Reveal request validation, an authoritative booking decision, persistence, and the response. Add notification as separate work after confirmation. Use numbered events and distinguish messages from elapsed time.
scenes.changed_condition: Lose the response after the booking has been stored. The user sees Unknown outcome while the stored record remains Confirmed. Compare this with a rejection before persistence. Preview status reconciliation without teaching the full retry mechanism yet. [S09]
scenes.principle: An interaction history explains why two apparently similar user symptoms can require different recovery actions.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the successful sequence and the lost-response sequence as two annotated panels.

scenes.instructor_title: Loading, empty, error, and success are different promises
scenes.visual_idea: A small interface state gallery with keyboard focus and text status indicators.
scenes.situation: Ask what “No rooms” means while a search is still loading. Reveal distinct Loading, Empty result, Validation error, Service unavailable, and Results states. Attach the promised meaning to each, rather than cycling through cosmetic designs.
scenes.changed_condition: Change one condition from an empty valid result to a failed request. Compare wording, available recovery actions, and focus movement. Make the distinction perceptible without color. [S25]
scenes.principle: An interface should communicate what is known and what the user can do next.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the state gallery with meaningful text alternatives and a recovery-action column.

scenes.instructor_title: A beautiful diagram can contradict the requirement
scenes.visual_idea: Three synchronized panels show R-01, a sequence diagram, and the calendar after the interaction.
scenes.situation: Present a sequence that sends Confirmed before deciding availability. Ask students to find the contradiction. Reveal the resulting overlapping calendar and the precise message order that permitted the false promise.
scenes.changed_condition: Move the confirmation message after the authoritative decision while leaving the other panels intact. Compare consistency across the representations rather than awarding correctness for diagram neatness.
scenes.principle: Models are useful when their claims can be checked against one another and against intended behavior.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the flawed sequence beside the corrected one, with the contradiction named.

scenes.instructor_title: A model is allowed to leave things out
scenes.visual_idea: A representation selector switches among context, sequence, state, and data views of one booking.
scenes.situation: Ask which view answers “Who owns B-001?” and which answers “What happened before the timeout?” Reveal the appropriate view without suggesting that it contains every implementation detail.
scenes.changed_condition: Change the audience from a student using the service to a maintainer investigating the failure. Compare the information each needs and the irrelevant detail each can omit.
scenes.principle: A useful abstraction preserves what matters for its question and makes its omissions intentional.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print a question-to-model matrix and the explicit limitations of each view.

weeks.title: DEVELOPMENT FLOW, UNCERTAINTY, AND ENGINEERING DECISIONS
weeks.question: Where is work waiting, and what would actually improve the flow?
outcomes: Distinguish iteration, increments, and a single large batch of delivery.
Locate a bottleneck using queues and completion evidence.
Distinguish work-in-progress, throughput, cycle time, and lead time.
Explain an estimate as conditional information rather than a guarantee.
Choose a next action using risk, dependency, feedback value, and capacity.

checks.question: Review processes one item per round. Will doubling implementation necessarily double completion?
checks.answer: No. Review remains the limiting stage in the stated model.

checks.question: What is the difference between iteration and increment?
checks.answer: Iteration revisits or refines understanding or a solution; an increment adds usable capability.

checks.question: Why might a risky assumption deserve attention before an easy visible feature?
checks.answer: Resolving it can prevent later work from relying on a false premise.

checks.question: What should accompany a process improvement claim?
checks.answer: A baseline, a stated change, a relevant outcome measure, and attention to quality or other side effects.

scenes.instructor_title: Eight finished parts can still be one late discovery
scenes.visual_idea: Two timelines compare one large batch with small usable slices; a requirement misunderstanding is revealed at a chosen feedback point.
scenes.situation: Ask when the team would learn that students need clear cancellation feedback. Reveal one timeline where everything is integrated at the end and another where a small booking-and-cancellation slice is inspected earlier. Explain the difference between adding usable capability and revising understanding.
scenes.changed_condition: Keep the misunderstanding constant but move the feedback point. Compare what must be reconsidered at that point. Then introduce a high-coordination integration constraint so students see that small slices still require thoughtful interfaces and sequencing.
scenes.principle: Shorter feedback loops can expose wrong assumptions earlier; useful increments must still make sense as a system.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the two timelines with discovery points, affected work, and stated assumptions.

scenes.instructor_title: A meeting does not create a feedback loop by itself
scenes.visual_idea: A three-column comparison of plan-driven coordination, iterative timeboxes, and flow-based policies.
scenes.situation: Ask what information each approach makes visible and when decisions change. Introduce Scrum through goals, inspection, and adaptation within its defined framework, and Kanban through explicit workflow, controlling work-in-progress, and improving flow. Do not claim a generic board is the whole of either. [S04, S05]
scenes.changed_condition: Change the work from a planned capability to unpredictable incident arrivals. Compare which coordination mechanisms help and what policies need revision; do not declare one universal winner.
scenes.principle: Choose coordination practices for the uncertainty and constraints of the work, not for their labels.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the comparison with a note that simplified lecture examples are not complete method definitions.

scenes.instructor_title: Making one stage faster can make the next queue longer
scenes.visual_idea: A work board and a numerical queue chart share the same discrete-round data.
scenes.situation: Run implementation at two cards per round and review at one. Ask where the next unfinished card will wait. Reveal the review queue accumulating, with completed work counted separately from work started. Let the class predict the result before doubling implementation capacity.
scenes.changed_condition: Change only implementation capacity to four and replay the same arrival schedule. Compare completion rate and queue length. Restore the baseline, then change review capacity to two. Explain that the bottleneck may move once a constraint is relieved.
scenes.principle: Local activity is not the same as system throughput; improve the limiting flow, not merely the busiest-looking stage.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print selected rounds and the corresponding queue/completion table, including capacities and transfer rules.

scenes.instructor_title: A shorter internal cycle can hide a longer external wait
scenes.visual_idea: Each card has arrival, start, and finish markers; a work-in-progress limit controls admission.
scenes.situation: Ask which clock a stakeholder experiences. Reveal lead time from request arrival to completion and cycle time from the declared start boundary to completion. Mark the difference visually and state the boundaries before using the terms. [S05]
scenes.changed_condition: Reduce allowed in-progress work while keeping demand constant. Compare internal work age and the queue waiting before admission. Avoid claiming that moving waiting outside the measurement boundary is a real improvement.
scenes.principle: Timing metrics are meaningful only when their boundaries and excluded waiting are explicit.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the time markers and both waits; retain the ready queue instead of cropping it away.

scenes.instructor_title: A precise number can be less honest than a range
scenes.visual_idea: An estimate range sits beside known work, dependencies, and unresolved questions.
scenes.situation: Ask whether “three days” means effort, elapsed time, or a commitment. Reveal the dependencies and review capacity behind the estimate. Compare a range based on several similar examples with a single unsupported number.
scenes.changed_condition: Change one assumption: the identity interface is not yet agreed. Widen or qualify the estimate and show the value of resolving that uncertainty. Do not turn fictional ranges into statistical confidence intervals without a model and data.
scenes.principle: An estimate is a conditional statement whose assumptions should travel with it.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the estimate with its assumptions and the condition that would trigger revision.

scenes.instructor_title: The most useful next step may be the one that reduces uncertainty
scenes.visual_idea: A decision table contrasts impact, uncertainty, reversibility, cost of delay, and information gained.
scenes.situation: Offer a visual refinement, a proof that simultaneous bookings cannot overlap, and an investigation into an unclear identity dependency. Ask what the team should learn before committing more work. Reveal what each step would clarify and what failure would cost.
scenes.changed_condition: Change only the reversibility of a decision: a temporary interface choice becomes a difficult data migration. Compare the amount of evidence worth seeking before proceeding. Use ordinal judgments and explanatory notes rather than multiplying invented probability scores.
scenes.principle: Prioritize not only output, but also the decisions and uncertainties that could make later work wasteful.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the decision table and a short rationale, including what remains uncertain.

scenes.instructor_title: “Coded” and “ready to rely on” are different claims
scenes.visual_idea: A work card accumulates evidence badges for intended behavior, review, checks, documentation, and operability.
scenes.situation: Ask whether a cancellation change should be considered complete when the happy-path function runs. Reveal missing ownership checks and missing user feedback. Introduce a shared completion policy appropriate to this team's risk.
scenes.changed_condition: Change the work to an internal wording correction with no behavioral effect. Compare the relevant evidence instead of demanding identical ceremony for every change. Distinguish acceptance of a particular requirement from a broader completion policy. [S04]
scenes.principle: A shared completion policy should make quality expectations visible and proportionate.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the two changes with their relevant evidence, not an unexplained universal checklist.

scenes.instructor_title: A process change is a hypothesis, too
scenes.visual_idea: Before-and-after panels connect a workflow observation, proposed change, measure, and possible side effect.
scenes.situation: Ask what should happen after noticing a long review queue. Reveal a proposal to share review work, the expected effect, and what would count as contrary evidence. Keep the discussion about the system rather than blaming an individual.
scenes.changed_condition: Increase review speed but show more missed issues. Compare throughput with quality and rework. Leave the class with the idea of a balanced improvement experiment rather than one target number.
scenes.principle: Change a process deliberately, observe its consequences, and revise the explanation when the evidence disagrees.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the process hypothesis and the before/after evidence with the side effect included.

weeks.title: MODULARITY, INTERFACES, AND THE COST OF CHANGE
weeks.question: When one requirement changes, which parts should need to change?
outcomes: Trace the effect of a requirement change through dependent components.
Distinguish cohesive responsibility from unrelated work gathered in one module.
Explain how an interface can hide changeable implementation details.
Recognize why fewer lines or more abstractions do not automatically mean better design.
Explain refactoring as structural change with preserved intended behavior.

checks.question: Why is a duplicated duration rule risky?
checks.answer: Copies can change inconsistently and create conflicting decisions.

checks.question: Does a centralized rule mean only one check is needed?
checks.answer: No. Different checks should still independently examine its important behavior and integration.

checks.question: Why did the replacement notifier break the design despite matching parameters?
checks.answer: It violated the expected failure behavior and affected confirmation.

checks.question: What should an architecture or design decision record preserve?
checks.answer: Context, alternatives, choice, consequences, and the assumptions or triggers that warrant revisiting it.

scenes.instructor_title: Two designs can look identical until something changes
scenes.visual_idea: Two matching booking screens above two different internal dependency maps.
scenes.situation: Ask whether the screens reveal which design will be easier to change. Reveal the internal responsibilities only after the class commits a prediction. Trace one successful request through each version.
scenes.changed_condition: Change the maximum booking duration while holding the screen and user goal constant. Stop before highlighting affected components so students identify likely edits first.
scenes.principle: Design quality becomes visible through the changes and failures a structure must accommodate.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print both internal maps with the same user-visible behavior stated above them.

scenes.instructor_title: Watch a single policy change spread
scenes.visual_idea: A stable dependency graph progressively marks changed files, required rechecks, and unaffected components using distinct symbols.
scenes.situation: In Design A, reduce the maximum duration from 120 to 90 minutes. Ask which components contain the rule and which merely consume its result. Reveal duplicated decisions in the browser, handler, and reminder code. Show a missed copy accepting a duration that another component rejects.
scenes.changed_condition: Apply the same change to Design B. Highlight the authoritative policy edit and the affected interface/tests, while leaving genuinely unrelated modules untouched. Compare edit locations, revalidation needs, and inconsistency risk; do not promise that one module means only one file ever changes.
scenes.principle: Useful boundaries localize decisions while keeping their dependents and evidence visible.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the baseline graphs and changed graphs with an edit/recheck/unaffected legend.

scenes.instructor_title: A module name is not a reason for its contents to belong together
scenes.visual_idea: Responsibility cards cluster by reason to change rather than by file extension.
scenes.situation: Show a “Utilities” module containing booking rules, email formatting, date display, and storage access. Ask which tasks change for the same reason. Reveal a regrouping around meaningful responsibilities.
scenes.changed_condition: Add a new notification format while keeping booking policy unchanged. Compare the groups affected before and after regrouping. Acknowledge that a boundary that separates tightly related behavior can also create unnecessary coordination.
scenes.principle: Cohesion concerns meaningful related responsibility, not simply making modules small.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the responsibility grouping and the change that explains each boundary.

scenes.instructor_title: A replacement fits only when its behavior fits
scenes.visual_idea: A component plugs into a labeled interface; inputs, outputs, errors, and side effects are shown as contract cards.
scenes.situation: Replace a notification implementation while keeping its call shape unchanged. Ask whether matching function names guarantees compatibility. Reveal differences in failure reporting, repeated delivery, and whether the call blocks confirmation. Use R-04 to state the relevant behavior.
scenes.changed_condition: Change only the error behavior of the replacement. Compare a clearly reported failed notification with an implementation that throws into the booking path and undoes the user promise. Introduce preconditions, outcomes, and error expectations without a long type-system lecture.
scenes.principle: An interface contract includes behavior and failure semantics, not just matching names or parameter lists.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the two contract cards and the mismatch that breaks substitutability.

scenes.instructor_title: Who should know about the replaceable detail?
scenes.visual_idea: A policy component and storage adapter exchange a small domain-shaped interface; dependency arrows are distinct from runtime message arrows.
scenes.situation: Ask whether the booking rule should depend on a particular database client's response shape. Reveal an interface describing the domain decision instead. Keep runtime calls visible on a separate line to avoid confusing execution with source-code dependency.
scenes.changed_condition: Change the storage implementation while preserving the required atomic booking behavior. Compare which code needs knowledge of the change and what must still be verified.
scenes.principle: Depend on the behavior a responsibility needs, and isolate details that change for other reasons.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the source dependency view and runtime interaction view with explicit legends.

scenes.instructor_title: Change the structure without quietly changing the promise
scenes.visual_idea: A short pseudocode excerpt transforms in small steps beside a fixed table of expected outcomes.
scenes.situation: Start with duplicated duration checks and several named examples. Ask whether extracting a policy function should alter the answers. Reveal each structural change, then replay the same normal, boundary, and invalid inputs. Name refactoring only after the behavior comparison.
scenes.changed_condition: Introduce an accidental inclusive-boundary error during one step. The 120-minute example changes outcome. Compare a structural intention with the actual behavioral effect and restore the correct condition. Explain that checks provide evidence, not a proof of all behavior.
scenes.principle: Refactoring should preserve intended observable behavior; small steps and relevant checks make deviations easier to locate.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print before/after pseudocode and the regression example that exposed the mistaken boundary.

scenes.instructor_title: A flexible design can still be unnecessarily complicated
scenes.visual_idea: A comparison matrix contrasts duplication, a small policy function, and a generic rule framework.
scenes.situation: Ask which option fits two clear policy rules and a small team. Reveal setup, understanding, extension, and debugging costs as qualitative judgments. Avoid invented precision or a decorative three-dimensional score surface.
scenes.changed_condition: Change one condition: several independently changing policies now exist. Revisit the decision and identify what evidence might justify more structure. Keep flexibility as a costed option, not a virtue without limits.
scenes.principle: Abstraction should earn its complexity by simplifying real responsibilities or plausible change.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the alternatives and the condition under which the recommendation changes.

scenes.instructor_title: A future maintainer needs the reason, not only the diagram
scenes.visual_idea: A compact decision record connects context, alternatives, choice, consequences, and revisit trigger.
scenes.situation: Ask what will be missing when a maintainer sees only “Use a Policy component.” Reveal why the boundary was chosen, what it deliberately does not generalize, and which assumptions could make the choice obsolete.
scenes.changed_condition: Change the scope from one campus to several with different rules. Compare blindly preserving the old decision with revisiting its stated trigger.
scenes.principle: A design decision is easier to maintain when its reasoning and limits are recorded.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the concise decision record with the relevant requirement IDs.

weeks.title: ARCHITECTURE, INTERACTIONS, AND DISTRIBUTED FAILURE
weeks.question: What changes when a dependency becomes slow, unavailable, or uncertain?
outcomes: Distinguish a module boundary from a process or deployment boundary.
Read context, component, and runtime views at an appropriate level.
Explain how a concurrent check-then-write can violate a shared invariant.
Distinguish timeout, failure, and unknown outcome.
Compare synchronous and asynchronous interactions, including their costs.

checks.question: Why can two availability checks both return true?
checks.answer: They can observe the same earlier state before either write has been enforced.

checks.question: Why not block confirmation on every notification attempt?
checks.answer: It couples the booking promise to an external dependency unnecessarily under R-04; separate work still needs reliable tracking.

checks.question: What should happen when an operation key is reused with a different payload?
checks.answer: A defined conflict or rejection, not silently treating the altered request as the original operation.

checks.question: Is a C4 container always a Docker container?
checks.answer: No. It denotes an application or data-store boundary in that model, not a specific packaging technology.

scenes.instructor_title: A box can mean a responsibility, a process, or a machine
scenes.visual_idea: A controlled zoom moves from system context to runtime containers to components, preserving labels and the current question.
scenes.situation: Ask what a box labeled Booking represents. Reveal three distinct meanings on separate views. Trace the same user request without pretending every component runs on its own server.
scenes.changed_condition: Move Notification into a separate worker while leaving Policy and Booking in one application. Compare what changed operationally with what stayed the same logically. [S08]
scenes.principle: Architecture views should state their level; logical separation does not automatically imply network separation.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the three labeled views with a brief legend defining each boundary.

scenes.instructor_title: Follow one request across real boundaries
scenes.visual_idea: A sequence diagram and runtime map highlight the same request ID, with latency segments and failure points.
scenes.situation: Ask which dependency the user is waiting for at each step. Reveal identity checking, policy validation, authoritative persistence, response, and later notification. Label the difference between a call that blocks the response and work that continues after it.
scenes.changed_condition: Make notification unavailable while preserving the authoritative store. Compare a design that makes all confirmation wait for email with one that records notification work separately. State the extra responsibility: pending delivery must be observable and recoverable, not merely forgotten.
scenes.principle: Interaction structure determines which failures affect which user promises.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the two request sequences with blocking and asynchronous steps labeled in text.

scenes.instructor_title: More deployable pieces create more boundaries to manage
scenes.visual_idea: A side-by-side architecture comparison and a qualitative trade-off table.
scenes.situation: Ask what a separate service buys a small team. Reveal possible independent release or scaling benefits beside network failures, contract coordination, data ownership, and operational work. Keep the single-application version modular rather than drawing it as an unstructured blob.
scenes.changed_condition: Change only one condition: notification volume grows independently of booking writes. Compare the targeted benefit of separating that workload with splitting every component.
scenes.principle: Choose deployment boundaries for demonstrated needs; modularity and distribution are different decisions.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print both alternatives and the changed condition, with no universal winner label.

scenes.instructor_title: Two individually sensible actions can violate one shared rule
scenes.visual_idea: Two request lanes advance through Read, Decide, and Write beside one room calendar.
scenes.situation: Pause after both requests read an available interval. Ask what each will decide. Reveal two confirmations in the naive check-then-write design. The key issue is the shared invariant, not which user clicked first by a few milliseconds.
scenes.changed_condition: Replace the separate check and write with an authoritative, atomic enforcement strategy for the no-overlap invariant. Step the same competing requests: one confirms, the other receives a conflict or retries appropriately. Explain that isolation choices, constraints, locking, and retries must be selected correctly; merely writing “transaction” around code is not a universal fix. [S10]
scenes.principle: An invariant shared by concurrent operations needs enforcement that survives their interleavings.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the violating interleaving and corrected interleaving with the invariant beside both.

scenes.instructor_title: A timeout does not tell us whether a write happened
scenes.visual_idea: A message timeline, an operation identifier, and a stored-result panel show a lost response and retry.
scenes.situation: Store B-001, then lose its response. Ask whether the requester should submit a new operation. Reveal how an unrecognized retry can create a duplicate logical action. Introduce an operation key scoped to the requester and intended action.
scenes.changed_condition: Retry with the same key and identical request. Compare a stable stored result with repeating the effect. Then change the payload while reusing the key and show an explicit conflict. Distinguish this application mechanism from assuming every HTTP POST is idempotent or that an “exactly once” guarantee appears automatically. [S09]
scenes.principle: Retries need defined semantics for identity, repeated effects, and uncertain outcomes.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the original request, lost response, repeated request, and reconciled result, including key scope.

scenes.instructor_title: A confirmed booking and a pending email can both be true
scenes.visual_idea: A booking record and a pending notification record advance on separate timelines.
scenes.situation: Ask whether delayed email means the booking failed. Reveal R-04: confirmation depends on the booking decision, while notification may complete later. Show pending, delivered, and failed-delivery observations without hiding them from support.
scenes.changed_condition: Duplicate a delivery attempt while keeping the booking unchanged. Compare a handler that tolerates repeat work with one that produces unintended extra effects. Mention a durable handoff pattern without requiring implementation detail.
scenes.principle: Asynchronous work changes the timing and failure contract; it does not remove responsibility for completion.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the two timelines and the user-facing meaning of each combination.

scenes.instructor_title: An added field and a changed meaning are not equivalent
scenes.visual_idea: A request/response contract appears beside old and new consumers.
scenes.situation: Ask whether adding a response field is always harmless. Reveal that compatibility depends on consumer behavior; strict consumers may reject additions. Contrast that with silently changing the meaning of an existing field.
scenes.changed_condition: Change a booking status representation and replay old and new consumers. Compare an explicit transition strategy with an abrupt breaking change.
scenes.principle: Compatibility is a relationship between actual producers and consumers, not a label on a release.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print a producer-consumer compatibility matrix with the assumptions behind each cell.

scenes.instructor_title: Choose the smallest structure that protects the required promises
scenes.visual_idea: A decision record ties quality scenarios, trade-offs, ownership, and failure behavior to one selected architecture.
scenes.situation: Ask which evidence supports the default architecture for this case. Reveal a modular application with an authoritative store and separately recoverable notification work as a teaching baseline, not a universal prescription.
scenes.changed_condition: Change the constraints to multiple independently operated campuses. Identify what must be reconsidered without pretending the current lecture has solved cross-region consistency.
scenes.principle: Architecture decisions should explain which requirements they protect and which assumptions would change the choice.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the decision record with the unresolved questions and revisit triggers.

weeks.title: COLLABORATION, VERSION HISTORY, AND REVIEWABLE CHANGE
weeks.question: How can several people change one system without losing intent or trust?
outcomes: Read a small commit graph and distinguish commits, branch references, and merges.
Explain the difference between a textual conflict and an incompatible behavioral change.
Identify the context and evidence needed to review a change.
Explain how dependency and configuration choices affect reproducibility.
Use history and decision records to explain why a change was made.

checks.question: What distinguishes a branch label from a commit?
checks.answer: A branch label points to a commit and can move; the recorded commit represents a particular snapshot and ancestry.

checks.question: Can two changes merge cleanly and still conflict?
checks.answer: Yes. Their behavior or assumptions can contradict even when the edited text does not overlap.

checks.question: What context should accompany a policy change?
checks.answer: The intended requirement, affected behavior, relevant design constraints, and checks demonstrating the change.

checks.question: Why record dependency inputs?
checks.answer: The same source can run differently when its resolved dependencies or configuration differ.

scenes.instructor_title: History is a graph of states and relationships
scenes.visual_idea: A commit graph grows one node at a time beside a tiny snapshot of the booking policy; branch labels move separately from nodes.
scenes.situation: Ask whether a branch is a second permanent copy of every file. Reveal commits as recorded snapshots linked to parent commits, then move a branch reference when a new commit is added. Draw time consistently but explain that graph ancestry, not horizontal position alone, determines the relationship. [S06]
scenes.changed_condition: Create a second line of development from the same ancestor. Compare two descendants with different changes, then reveal a merge with two parents. Contrast a fast-forward case without suggesting that every integration needs a merge commit.
scenes.principle: History records relationships between changes; branch names are movable references, not the changes themselves.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the common ancestor, divergent descendants, and merged state in three labeled panels.

scenes.instructor_title: A conflict asks for a decision about meaning
scenes.visual_idea: Two edits to one policy line appear beside the requirement they were intended to implement.
scenes.situation: Ask whether taking the left or right version is sufficient. Reveal one edit implementing the 90-minute variant and another reorganizing the same validation. Show the shared original so the class can distinguish changed behavior from changed structure.
scenes.changed_condition: Resolve the text while accidentally losing the upper bound. Compare a syntactically valid result with a requirement-based resolution that preserves both the intended rule and the structural improvement. Reveal the boundary check that detects the mistake.
scenes.principle: A merge resolution must reconcile intent and verify the combined behavior, not merely remove conflict markers.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print ancestor, two edits, chosen resolution, and the verification result with compact annotations.

scenes.instructor_title: No conflict does not mean no contradiction
scenes.visual_idea: A clean-merge indicator sits above a policy value and a user message that disagree.
scenes.situation: Ask whether a successful merge means the feature is ready. Reveal a policy rejecting durations above 90 while the newly added message still says 120. The files differ, so the version-control tool had no textual disagreement to flag.
scenes.changed_condition: Replace the duplicated message value with a response derived from the same approved policy source. Compare the user-visible behavior before and after the change.
scenes.principle: Textual integration and semantic integration are different kinds of evidence.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the clean merge and the contradictory outcomes; do not leave only the green merge indicator.

scenes.instructor_title: A diff is easier to judge when the claim is visible
scenes.visual_idea: A review panel connects requirement, diff, checks, decision rationale, and focused comments.
scenes.situation: Show the diff alone and ask what a reviewer cannot yet decide. Reveal the purpose, affected rule, alternatives, and checks. Sort comments into correctness, security, design, understandability, and optional preference. Explain that automated style checks can reduce distraction, not replace judgment. [S07]
scenes.changed_condition: Split an unrelated rename out of the same change. Compare the reviewer’s task with and without the unrelated material, without claiming an exact universal speed improvement. Keep one substantive concern unresolved until its supporting evidence appears. AI beat: label the same diff as drafted by an automated assistant with the description “fix stuff”. Ask what changes for the reviewer. Nothing: the requirement, the checks and the rationale are still required, and the empty description is the documentation failure of scene 07 arriving early.
scenes.principle: Review is an evidence-based conversation about a change, not a vote on how convincing its author sounds.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the compact review packet and two example comments with their supporting reasons.

scenes.instructor_title: Distance from shared reality can grow quietly
scenes.visual_idea: Two timelines show the same intended changes integrated in small steps or accumulated on a long-lived branch.
scenes.situation: Ask where incompatibilities would become visible. Reveal the integration points and overlapping assumptions, not just the number of commits. Explain that smaller steps still need useful checks and a safe way to keep unfinished behavior unavailable.
scenes.changed_condition: Introduce one contract change halfway through both timelines. Compare when each branch learns about it. Avoid presenting one branching convention as mandatory for every team.
scenes.principle: Choose a collaboration strategy that exposes incompatible assumptions early enough to act on them.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print both timelines with the contract-change event and discovery points.

scenes.instructor_title: A source snapshot is only part of a reproducible run
scenes.visual_idea: A source revision connects to dependency versions, runtime, configuration, data fixture, and build artifact.
scenes.situation: Ask why the same code might behave differently on two machines. Reveal one changed dependency and one different configuration value. Distinguish a recorded version constraint from the actual resolved dependency set.
scenes.changed_condition: Hold the source fixed and restore the declared dependency and configuration inputs. Compare repeatability of the teaching result. Keep secrets out of the diagram and out of the repository; use placeholder references.
scenes.principle: Reproducibility requires control of the relevant inputs, not just possession of the source files.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the input manifest and the single difference responsible for the changed behavior.

scenes.instructor_title: The reason for a change should survive the conversation
scenes.visual_idea: A short change description and decision record are linked to the commit and requirement.
scenes.situation: Ask what a maintainer learns from “fix stuff.” Reveal an alternative explaining the observed problem, intended behavior, and a constraint that ruled out an obvious solution. Separate durable rationale from a transcript of every discussion.
scenes.changed_condition: Remove the original author from the scenario. Compare how much each record helps a future reviewer understand whether the constraint still applies.
scenes.principle: Documentation earns its place by preserving information that cannot be reliably reconstructed from the code.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the weak and improved descriptions with the useful information highlighted in words.

scenes.instructor_title: Shared confidence comes from several kinds of evidence
scenes.visual_idea: A change card collects review, checks, integration status, and remaining uncertainty without turning them into a numerical score.
scenes.situation: Ask which missing evidence prevents this change from being integrated responsibly. Reveal that passing checks does not settle an unresolved authorization question, while approval does not fix a failing integration check.
scenes.changed_condition: Resolve the actual concern, rerun the affected checks, and compare the evidence packet. Restore the canonical 120-minute policy and show that later weeks use that baseline.
scenes.principle: Integration readiness is a justified judgment about the change and its context, not a single green indicator.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the final evidence packet and an explicit baseline-restoration note.

weeks.title: TESTING BEHAVIOR AND BUILDING CREDIBLE EVIDENCE
weeks.question: Which checks would challenge our assumptions rather than merely repeat them?
outcomes: Derive ordinary, boundary, and invalid cases from a stated rule.
Choose a suitable scope for a check and explain what it leaves unexamined.
Distinguish executing code from asserting the intended result.
Explain a property and a small mutation-based challenge to a test suite.
Recognize shared assumptions, uncontrolled inputs, and flaky observations.

checks.question: Which two cases distinguish an inclusive 120-minute limit from no upper limit?
checks.answer: 120 must be accepted and 121 rejected, under otherwise valid conditions.

checks.question: Do adjacent intervals overlap under the course rule?
checks.answer: No. The end of one may equal the start of the next because the intervals are half-open.

checks.question: Why test the storage boundary as well as the overlap function?
checks.answer: Correct local arithmetic alone does not protect the invariant against concurrent operations.

checks.question: Why can implementation and test agree while both are wrong?
checks.answer: They may share the same mistaken assumption or calculate the expected result using the defective logic.

scenes.instructor_title: One passing example can hide the wrong boundary
scenes.visual_idea: Input cards move through a small predicate; accepted and rejected outcomes are shown beside the requirement.
scenes.situation: Run 60 minutes and ask whether the rule is implemented correctly. Reveal that both the correct and incorrect comparisons pass this example. Step through 119, then pause before 120. Ask for a prediction before revealing the rejection caused by the exclusive upper bound.
scenes.changed_condition: Change only the comparison to inclusive and replay the same cases. Compare 120 and 121 so the fix does not accidentally remove the upper limit.
scenes.principle: Test cases should distinguish plausible incorrect behavior from the intended behavior.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the rule, both predicates, and the completed six-case boundary table.

scenes.instructor_title: Input categories make omissions easier to see
scenes.visual_idea: A number line and a small two-dimensional table separate valid durations, too-short values, too-long values, and malformed or reversed intervals.
scenes.situation: Ask whether testing every minute is the only way to gain confidence. Reveal categories with shared expectations, then focus attention on boundaries where the decision changes. Add invalid input shape and end-before-start as different concerns from an out-of-range duration.
scenes.changed_condition: Change the rule to the explicitly labeled 90-minute variant. Compare which cases remain useful and which boundary cases must change, then restore 120.
scenes.principle: Partitions organize expectations; boundaries expose where one expectation becomes another.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the baseline partitions and a small variant annotation without mixing their expected outcomes.

scenes.instructor_title: Different checks answer different questions
scenes.visual_idea: A layered system view highlights a pure policy function, component interaction, storage enforcement, and complete user journey.
scenes.situation: Ask whether a unit check of overlap arithmetic proves that concurrent requests cannot double-book. Reveal the missing shared-storage behavior. Place focused function checks, integration checks, and a complete booking journey where they observe their respective claims.
scenes.changed_condition: Replace the real notification boundary with a controlled test double. Compare faster isolation of booking behavior with the remaining uncertainty about actual integration. Show a separate contract or integration check for that uncertainty.
scenes.principle: The appropriate test scope follows the claim and failure risk, not the prestige of a test label.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print a claim-to-check-scope matrix with one explicit limitation per row.

scenes.instructor_title: The expected answer needs its own justification
scenes.visual_idea: Requirement, implementation, and expected-result cards form a triangle; a copied assumption is visibly traced through two cards.
scenes.situation: Show a test whose expected value is calculated by the same incorrect helper used in production. Ask why agreement is weak evidence. Reveal an independently derived expectation from the stated rule and a hand-checked interval example.
scenes.changed_condition: Change the shared helper while leaving the requirement fixed. Compare the self-confirming test with the independent check that detects the discrepancy. AI beat: name the case where the tests and the helper were drafted by the same assistant from the same misreading of R-02. Their agreement is this loop again. Week 13 returns to it as the shared-assumption scene.
scenes.principle: A test oracle—the basis for the expected result—must not simply repeat the defect being examined.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the dependency of each expected result and the independent derivation.

scenes.instructor_title: A useful property describes more than one example
scenes.visual_idea: A calendar receives a controlled sequence of candidate intervals; a property panel shows whether confirmed bookings overlap.
scenes.situation: Ask what should remain true after any accepted booking. Reveal the no-overlap invariant and several generated-but-fixed examples, including adjacency. Explain that property-based tools can explore many cases and help reduce a failure to a smaller counterexample. [S11]
scenes.changed_condition: Change the overlap predicate from strict interval intersection to a comparison that also rejects adjacency. Replay [10:00,11:00) and [11:00,12:00). Compare the property about disallowing real overlaps with a separate property that valid adjacent bookings remain possible.
scenes.principle: Properties expose classes of behavior, but the properties themselves must express the intended rule.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the properties, deterministic examples, and smallest displayed counterexample; retain half-open interval notation.

scenes.instructor_title: Executed is not the same as checked
scenes.visual_idea: A coverage overlay sits beside assertions; a one-character mutation changes a boundary while execution remains similar.
scenes.situation: Ask what a highlighted executed line tells us. Reveal that a test can reach the line without asserting the result that matters. Introduce mutation as intentionally changing behavior to ask whether a suite notices. [S12]
scenes.changed_condition: Use the exclusive-boundary mutation and first omit the 120-minute case, then add it. Compare surviving and detected changes. Mention that equivalent or irrelevant mutations can require judgment; a mutation score is not a proof of correctness.
scenes.principle: Coverage and mutation results are diagnostic signals about evidence, not substitutes for requirements.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the mutation, missing case, added assertion, and the limited conclusion supported by the result.

scenes.instructor_title: A moving clock can make a stable rule look unreliable
scenes.visual_idea: Two runs share the same code but use different clocks or uncontrolled message timing; the fixture inputs are displayed.
scenes.situation: Ask why “cancel before the start time” sometimes passes and sometimes fails. Reveal that the wall clock crossed the boundary between runs. Replace it with an explicit teaching clock and deterministic dependency behavior.
scenes.changed_condition: Keep the clock fixed and inject one genuine notification failure. Compare a repeatable meaningful failure with a test that randomly waits for enough time to pass.
scenes.principle: Control irrelevant variation so a failing check tells us something about the behavior being examined.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the uncontrolled inputs, controlled fixture, and the rule-specific result.

scenes.instructor_title: A check can guide a change and later guard its meaning
scenes.visual_idea: A short requirement-to-failing-check-to-small-change-to-recheck loop ends with a refactoring comparison.
scenes.situation: Ask what should happen before fixing the exclusive upper bound. Reveal a focused failing check, a minimal correction, and rerun evidence. Explain test-first development as one way to make the expected behavior explicit, not a guarantee of good requirements.
scenes.changed_condition: Refactor the corrected predicate without changing its contract. Compare unchanged behavior under the checks while acknowledging untested conditions and higher-level integration evidence.
scenes.principle: Tests are feedback instruments whose value depends on the claims, observations, and assumptions they preserve.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the feedback loop and a final claim-evidence-remaining-uncertainty table.

weeks.title: SECURITY, PRIVACY, AND TRUSTWORTHY DEPENDENCIES
weeks.question: What must remain true when a request, dependency, or assumption cannot be trusted?
outcomes: Identify an asset, trust boundary, threat, and proposed mitigation in a simple system.
Distinguish authentication from authorization and apply ownership rules.
Explain why validation and authoritative enforcement belong at trusted boundaries.
Compare useful diagnostics with unnecessary personal-data exposure.
Explain what dependency inventory and provenance evidence do and do not establish.

checks.question: May U-02 cancel a future booking owned by U-01 in the baseline?
checks.answer: No. Authentication alone does not satisfy the ownership requirement.

checks.question: Why is a request identifier preferable to a full private message in this diagnostic example?
checks.answer: It can connect relevant observations while avoiding content that is unnecessary for the stated support question.

checks.question: What does a component inventory establish?
checks.answer: Which recorded components are included or expected within its defined scope; it does not by itself establish that they are safe.

checks.question: Should notification failure automatically cancel an already confirmed booking?
checks.answer: No. Under R-04 the booking remains confirmed while notification work is explicitly pending or failed and recoverable.

scenes.instructor_title: What are we trying to protect, and from whom?
scenes.visual_idea: A data-flow diagram marks booking records, identity assertions, browser input, storage, and notification boundaries.
scenes.situation: Ask which arrows carry information the service can accept without checking. Reveal that user-supplied room, time, and booking identifiers are claims, not authority. Identify unwanted outcomes: false cancellation, data disclosure, denied service, and misleading state.
scenes.changed_condition: Change one condition: the browser sends a different booking identifier while the authenticated identity remains U-02. Follow the request across the same boundary and ask which decision must stop an unauthorized effect.
scenes.principle: Threat modeling connects a protected outcome to an entry point, an assumption, and a concrete control.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the boundary diagram and a small asset-threat-control table with residual questions.

scenes.instructor_title: Being signed in does not authorize every action
scenes.visual_idea: A decision matrix shows requester, owner, booking state, future start time, and cancellation result.
scenes.situation: Ask whether U-02 may cancel B-001 simply because the request is authenticated. Reveal R-03: only the authenticated owner may cancel their own future confirmed booking in the baseline. Show the permission decision next to the requested state transition.
scenes.changed_condition: Change only the requester to U-01, then separately change the booking to already started. Compare these independent conditions. A staff closure role does not silently grant a cancellation override; any delegation would be an explicitly revised policy.
scenes.principle: Authentication establishes an identity claim; authorization decides whether that identity may perform this action on this resource.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the full decision matrix, including same-user but too-late rejection.

scenes.instructor_title: A disabled button is guidance, not a security boundary
scenes.visual_idea: A polished interface sits above a service-side decision point; both paths converge on the same authoritative rule.
scenes.situation: Ask whether hiding the Cancel button prevents an unauthorized request. Reveal that the service still receives requests independently of the visible interface. The trusted boundary must check identity, ownership, state, and time rather than relying on the button.
scenes.changed_condition: Bypass only the interface affordance in the illustration, without showing attack tooling. Compare a service that trusts supplied ownership with one that obtains ownership from the protected booking record.
scenes.principle: User-interface constraints help users, while trusted enforcement protects the rule when those constraints are absent.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the two paths and the same required service-side decision.

scenes.instructor_title: Input should not acquire unintended authority
scenes.visual_idea: A structured request is separated into data fields and the operation interpreting them; a small query-template diagram illustrates the boundary.
scenes.situation: Ask what could go wrong when a text value becomes part of the instructions used to access storage. Reveal the conceptual distinction between validated data, parameterized operations, and authorization. Explain that none replaces the other. [S13]
scenes.changed_condition: Keep the text value unchanged and change only how the operation treats it: as structure or as data. Compare the interpretation without providing an operational exploitation sequence. AI beat: the same boundary holds when the reader is an automated assistant. A note inside a file it reads is data, not an instruction to the reader. Week 13 examines that case as prompt injection.
scenes.principle: Validate the domain, preserve the data-versus-instruction boundary, and independently check permission.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the structured-data illustration with the three distinct responsibilities labeled.

scenes.instructor_title: Useful evidence does not require collecting everything
scenes.visual_idea: Two incident records are compared field by field, linked to the actual support question.
scenes.situation: Ask which fields distinguish a failed notification from a failed booking. Reveal that a request identifier, outcome category, and dependency status may answer the question without a message body or private meeting description. Mark fictional identifiers as pseudonymous, not magically anonymous.
scenes.changed_condition: Add a narrowly justified diagnostic need and choose the minimal additional field, access restriction, and retention rationale. Compare purposeful collection with permanent detailed logging by default.
scenes.principle: Diagnostic value, access, retention, and disclosure risk should be considered together.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the before-and-after records and a field-purpose-retention rationale table, without real personal information.

scenes.instructor_title: A component brings dependencies and assumptions with it
scenes.visual_idea: A dependency graph expands one level, then an inventory and build-provenance card attach to the selected release.
scenes.situation: Ask whether knowing the name of a direct library tells us everything included in a build. Reveal a transitive dependency. Explain an inventory or software bill of materials as visibility into components, and provenance as evidence about an artifact’s production. [S16]
scenes.changed_condition: Change one dependency version while keeping application source fixed. Compare the need to evaluate the new component, rebuild under controlled inputs, and recheck affected behavior. A familiar name, inventory entry, or signature alone does not prove safety. Licensing beat: change only the license of the transitive dependency in the fictional chain, from a permissive license to a copyleft license with a source-availability obligation. Compare what the license inventory now requires before release. Use SPDX identifiers as the vocabulary and keep this an engineering question about obligations and inventory, not legal advice. [S42]
scenes.principle: Supply-chain evidence makes dependencies inspectable; it does not eliminate the need for risk judgment and verification.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the exact fictional dependency set, the changed node, and the bounded claims of each evidence type. Add the license column with the changed identifier.

scenes.instructor_title: Failure behavior can preserve or violate the promise
scenes.visual_idea: A permission check, booking write, and notification step each receive a separate failure card.
