scenes.situation: Ask whether every failure should have the same response. Reveal that an unavailable permission decision must not silently grant access, while an email failure must not undo a confirmed booking under R-04. State the protected property at each boundary.
scenes.changed_condition: Move the failure from notification to authorization while keeping the request fixed. Compare safe outcomes and user messages rather than applying a blanket “always continue” or “always roll back everything” rule.
scenes.principle: Handling failure safely requires knowing which promise each operation is responsible for preserving.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print a failure-location-to-safe-outcome table with R-03 and R-04 references.

scenes.instructor_title: Security evidence belongs throughout the lifecycle
scenes.visual_idea: The familiar lifecycle loop receives threat questions, permission checks, review, dependency evidence, and incident feedback.
scenes.situation: Ask whether a final scanner can discover an unstated ownership policy. Reveal distinct contributions from requirements, design, implementation checks, review, release integrity, and operation. Use a small selected set of risks rather than reciting a top-ten list.
scenes.changed_condition: Introduce a new delegated-cancellation policy as an explicit hypothetical. Trace which model, checks, review questions, and diagnostic fields must be reconsidered before restoring the baseline.
scenes.principle: Security is maintained through connected decisions and feedback, not added by one tool at the end.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the lifecycle evidence map and the policy-change trace.

weeks.title: AUTOMATED DELIVERY AND EVIDENCE-BASED RELEASE
weeks.question: What evidence should travel with a change before it reaches users?
outcomes: Explain continuous integration, continuous delivery, and continuous deployment without tying them to a vendor.
Identify which evidence a release gate provides and its limitations.
Explain why the tested artifact and production artifact must be related unambiguously.
Compare deployment, user exposure, rollback, and forward recovery.
Interpret a small balanced set of delivery measures with explicit denominators.

checks.question: What is the distinction between continuous delivery and continuous deployment here?
checks.answer: A releasable state with an explicit production decision versus automatic production deployment of changes that pass the declared gates.

checks.question: Why keep configuration visible when promoting one artifact?
checks.answer: Configuration can change behavior independently of artifact identity.

checks.question: What is the change fail rate in the ten-deployment fixture?
checks.answer: Two of ten deployments required immediate intervention, so the rate is 20%.

checks.question: Does a notification already delivered disappear after code rollback?
checks.answer: No. External effects need their own reconciliation or compensating behavior.

scenes.instructor_title: A release path should make its evidence visible
scenes.visual_idea: A change token moves through integration, build, focused checks, broader checks, artifact recording, and release decision; evidence cards remain attached.
scenes.situation: Ask which stage would catch the incorrect 120-minute boundary and which would check ownership. Reveal distinct checks and pause at a failure. The token cannot advance merely because the animation has reached its next step. Explain that gate placement follows risk and feedback needs.
scenes.changed_condition: Fix the boundary but introduce an authorization regression. Replay the same pipeline and compare which evidence changes. Show a passing gate with an explicit scope label so it is not mistaken for a universal guarantee. AI beat: let the second change be proposed by an automated assistant. It enters the same path and is blocked by the same gate. Proposing a change and passing a gate are different authorities, which Week 13 develops as bounded action.
scenes.principle: Automation should preserve the connection between a claim, a check, its result, and the change being released.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the successful path and blocked path with the exact failed condition and artifact identity.

scenes.instructor_title: Integration, readiness, and deployment are different decisions
scenes.visual_idea: Three lanes distinguish frequent integration, a releasable state, and automatic production deployment.
scenes.situation: Ask whether automatically running tests is the whole meaning of continuous integration. Reveal frequent integration into shared work with useful checks. Contrast a system kept ready for release with one that automatically deploys changes passing the declared gates.
scenes.changed_condition: Add an explicit human release decision without changing build and verification automation. Compare continuous delivery with continuous deployment; neither label determines whether the underlying checks are sufficient.
scenes.principle: Describe which decision is automated rather than using “continuous” as a synonym for fast or safe.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the three lanes and identify the production-release decision in each.

scenes.instructor_title: Release the thing you checked, with the intended settings
scenes.visual_idea: A recorded artifact travels through environments while configuration cards remain separate and visible.
scenes.situation: Ask whether rebuilding from the same source later necessarily gives the same result. Reveal a changed resolved dependency. Compare promoting the recorded artifact with silently rebuilding an unverified one. Keep provenance evidence distinct from functional correctness. [S16]
scenes.changed_condition: Hold artifact identity fixed and change a configuration value affecting authorization or a dependency endpoint. Compare why environment-specific configuration still needs validation, even when the artifact is unchanged. Secrets remain references, never visible values.
scenes.principle: Artifact identity controls one source of uncertainty; configuration and environment behavior still need evidence.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the source-to-artifact relationship and the two configuration outcomes.

scenes.instructor_title: Installed code and visible behavior can change at different times
scenes.visual_idea: A release appears in the runtime map while a feature flag and a small cohort control exposure.
scenes.situation: Ask whether deploying code must expose a new behavior to everyone immediately. Reveal a disabled path, then a labeled small-cohort rollout. Make clear that hidden code is still deployed and may carry operational or security implications.
scenes.changed_condition: Change cohort size while holding the artifact fixed. Compare observations from a narrow rollout with the uncertainty about other users and workloads. A small cohort is not automatically representative.
scenes.principle: Separating deployment from exposure can create additional decision points, provided the controls and observations are trustworthy.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print deployment state, exposure state, and cohort assumptions in a small matrix.

scenes.instructor_title: Undoing code does not necessarily undo effects
scenes.visual_idea: A deployment timeline sits beside database compatibility and already-sent notifications.
scenes.situation: Ask whether returning to the previous binary restores the previous world. Reveal records written in a new format and messages already delivered. Compare a reversible code change with an irreversible external effect or incompatible schema change.
scenes.changed_condition: Use a compatibility-preserving transition that lets the earlier application continue reading data, then compare rollback feasibility. Where reversal is not safe, show a forward correction and explicit reconciliation rather than a magical rewind.
scenes.principle: Recovery must account for state, compatibility, and external effects—not only the application version.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the before-and-after state and a recovery-choice table with prerequisites.

scenes.instructor_title: Count outcomes without turning one number into the goal
scenes.visual_idea: A deployment timeline feeds five small numerical summaries with the observation window and denominators visible.
scenes.situation: Ask whether twice as many deployments necessarily means better delivery. Reveal the ten-deployment fixture and calculate the measures from the event records. Distinguish a failed deployment from an unplanned deployment that repairs an incident; they contribute to different numerators. [S17]
scenes.changed_condition: Split an otherwise identical release into several bookkeeping deployments. Compare the inflated count with unchanged user value and other evidence. Explain why an honest interpretation needs context, stable definitions, and several measures.
scenes.principle: Measures support improvement when their definitions and consequences remain visible.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the event table, five results, and explicit limits of the synthetic comparison.

scenes.instructor_title: Passing gates does not end verification
scenes.visual_idea: The release path loops back from user outcomes and service observations to earlier checks and requirements.
scenes.situation: Ask what happens when production traffic differs from the test fixture. Reveal a slow path absent from the earlier workload. Connect the observation to a new representative check and a revised capacity assumption rather than blaming the pipeline for not predicting everything.
scenes.changed_condition: Change only the workload mix. Compare why the same release artifact can behave differently and what additional evidence would distinguish code, configuration, and demand effects.
scenes.principle: Production feedback can refine the evidence model without making earlier checks pointless.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the release-to-observation-to-improved-check loop.

scenes.instructor_title: Ready means the remaining risk has been considered
scenes.visual_idea: A concise release record combines intended behavior, checked artifact, known limitations, exposure plan, and recovery conditions.
scenes.situation: Ask what the release decision-maker still needs beyond a green build. Reveal the affected users, compatibility constraints, monitoring question, and recovery plan. Keep the record brief enough to read while explaining.
scenes.changed_condition: Remove a safe recovery path from the scenario. Compare how that changes the required evidence and exposure decision even when the tests remain unchanged.
scenes.principle: Release readiness is an evidence-based decision under stated risk, not a decorative status badge.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the release record with the missing-evidence variant and its effect on the decision.

weeks.title: RELIABILITY, OBSERVABILITY, AND PERFORMANCE REASONING
weeks.question: Which observation would help distinguish the possible causes of a failure?
outcomes: Define an eligible event, a good event, an indicator, and an objective for a specific service promise.
Interpret a latency distribution without relying only on its average.
Use correlated observations to distinguish plausible incident causes.
Explain how retries can increase load and why recovery controls need conditions.
Separate immediate mitigation from later causal learning.

checks.question: What is the observed good-event rate for the declared fixture?
checks.answer: 980 divided by 1,000, or 98%.

checks.question: How many bad events does the illustrative 99% objective allow in that window?
checks.answer: Ten of 1,000; twenty are observed, so consumption is twice the allowance.

checks.question: Which signal helps locate where one request spent time?
checks.answer: A correlated trace can localize time across the observed request path, within its sampling and instrumentation limits.

checks.question: Why might a high CPU reading not justify an urgent incident alert by itself?
checks.answer: Its significance depends on user impact, capacity risk, and an actionable response, not the number alone.

scenes.instructor_title: A successful status code is not the complete promise
scenes.visual_idea: Request tokens enter a good/bad classification table with eligibility, correctness, and timing visible.
scenes.situation: Ask whether every rejected booking request is a service failure. Reveal a timely correct conflict response as a good outcome under this objective. Then classify a fast incorrect confirmation and a correct response arriving too late. The class must state the event definition before seeing the percentage. [S21]
scenes.changed_condition: Change only the observation: 20 of 1,000 eligible requests miss the promise. Compare 98% observed good events with the illustrative 99% objective. Explain the ten-event allowance and twenty-event consumption without treating the allowance as permission to ignore harmful failures.
scenes.principle: A reliability indicator is meaningful only after the user promise, event population, and observation window are defined.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the classifications, arithmetic, window, and objective; retain rejected-but-correct examples.

scenes.instructor_title: The average can hide the experience we need to improve
scenes.visual_idea: Two empirical latency distributions share axes and units; mean and nearest-rank p95 markers are shown separately.
scenes.situation: Ask whether equal averages imply equally responsive service. Reveal Dataset A: twenty requests at 200 ms. Dataset B: eighteen at 100 ms and two at 1,100 ms. Both average 200 ms, but their nearest-rank p95 values differ: 200 ms and 1,100 ms.
scenes.changed_condition: Change the comparison from the average to the tail, keeping the data fixed. Connect the result to the specific Q-01 fixture without claiming that twenty synthetic points establish real production performance.
scenes.principle: Use a distribution and a defined percentile method when the question concerns uneven user experience.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the sorted values or frequency table, both charts, sample sizes, and percentile method.

scenes.instructor_title: Each signal answers a different part of the question
scenes.visual_idea: One request timeline links a latency measurement, structured log entry, and distributed trace; selecting the request highlights matching records.
scenes.situation: Ask whether a spike in aggregate latency identifies the slow component. Reveal a trace with an unusually long storage wait, then a relevant event record. Contrast what the metric suggests, what the trace localizes, and what the log explains. [S20]
scenes.changed_condition: Change the cause to delayed notification that is not on the confirmation path. Compare the same user report with the request trace, showing why correlation and a clear interaction model matter.
scenes.principle: Telemetry becomes useful evidence when it connects a symptom to a discriminating question about the system.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the correlated packet with a shared request identifier and a caption for what each signal supports.

scenes.instructor_title: A plausible story needs a distinguishing observation
scenes.visual_idea: Three candidate causes sit beside predicted observations and the evidence actually available.
scenes.situation: Offer slow storage, an identity dependency failure, and exhausted request capacity. Ask which observation would separate them. Reveal one trace segment and one queue measurement, then eliminate only the hypotheses contradicted by that evidence.
scenes.changed_condition: Remove the trace sample from the packet. Compare the weaker conclusion now justified. A missing log entry is not automatically proof that an event never happened; collection may be incomplete.
scenes.principle: Diagnosis advances by testing predictions and acknowledging gaps, not by naming the first familiar cause.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the hypothesis-prediction-evidence table and the remaining uncertainty.

scenes.instructor_title: Trying harder can increase the pressure on a failing dependency
scenes.visual_idea: A controlled queue model shows original requests and separately labeled retry attempts; arrival and completion rates are visible.
scenes.situation: Start with a constrained dependency and ask whether immediate repeated retries will reduce waiting. Reveal extra attempts entering the same limited capacity, with no invented promise about exact real-world timings. Preserve the distinction between unique user operations and repeated attempts.
scenes.changed_condition: Change to bounded retries with delay, backoff, and an explicit timeout budget; show a circuit-open state as a deliberate temporary refusal to call the unhealthy dependency. Compare queue pressure and successful outcomes under the declared toy model. Keep jitter optional and seeded for reproducible teaching.
scenes.principle: Recovery behavior must account for shared capacity and the possibility that an earlier attempt already had an effect.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the baseline and bounded-retry model, assumptions, and reminder of Week 6 idempotency.

scenes.instructor_title: Restoring a useful service and explaining a cause are different jobs
scenes.visual_idea: An incident timeline separates detect, assess impact, mitigate, verify recovery, communicate, and investigate.
scenes.situation: Ask whether the team must know the complete cause before reducing harm. Reveal a safe exposure rollback or capacity protection, then show the evidence used to verify improvement. Keep user communication accurate about known impact and uncertainty.
scenes.changed_condition: Make code rollback unsafe because of state compatibility. Compare an alternative mitigation that limits exposure or degrades a nonessential capability without breaking the booking invariant.
scenes.principle: Incident response should reduce harm, preserve evidence, and keep claims proportionate to what is known.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the timeline and the reason the selected mitigation was safe in this scenario.

scenes.instructor_title: An alert should help someone decide what to do
scenes.visual_idea: A noisy stream of low-level alerts is contrasted with a user-impact signal and a short response guide.
scenes.situation: Ask whether every CPU fluctuation should interrupt someone. Reveal the user promise, the affected service, an actionable condition, and a next diagnostic question. Avoid prescribing a universal threshold independent of workload. [S22]
scenes.changed_condition: Hold resource utilization high while user outcomes remain acceptable, then lower it while correctness fails. Compare resource observations with the actual service objective.
scenes.principle: Alerting should connect a meaningful condition to an appropriate response, not merely report that a number changed.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the signal-condition-response relationship and the two counterexamples.

scenes.instructor_title: The explanation should improve the system, not find a scapegoat
scenes.visual_idea: A causal timeline connects conditions, decisions, observations, and follow-through checks.
scenes.situation: Ask what “someone made a mistake” fails to explain. Reveal missing safeguards, misleading feedback, or an untested workload assumption. Separate observed facts from hypotheses and identify which change would reduce recurrence or shorten detection.
scenes.changed_condition: Add a proposed action that sounds reassuring but cannot be verified. Compare it with a specific change, an owner role, and evidence showing whether the risk was reduced.
scenes.principle: Learning from an incident requires testable improvements to the conditions that shaped it.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the factual timeline and improvement-to-verification map without personal blame.

weeks.title: MAINTENANCE, EVOLUTION, AND SUSTAINABLE CHANGE
weeks.question: How can a useful system change without losing the behavior people rely on?
outcomes: Distinguish observed existing behavior from intended required behavior.
Explain a compatibility-preserving data transition and its recovery conditions.
Identify the future change cost and risk represented by a specific debt item.
Prioritize maintenance using evidence about impact, uncertainty, and reversibility.
Compare resource use per successful task without overstating environmental conclusions.

checks.question: When may the old representation be removed safely in the depicted transition?
checks.answer: After relevant consumers and stored data have migrated, compatibility evidence is sufficient, and recovery implications are understood.

checks.question: Is fixing an incorrect boundary a pure refactoring?
checks.answer: No. It intentionally changes externally observable behavior to satisfy the rule.

checks.question: What makes a debt item actionable?
checks.answer: A specific deferred cost or risk, the conditions that cause it, a possible change, and evidence for its priority.

checks.question: What is the resource reduction in the declared fixture?
checks.answer: Reads per successful search decrease from 10 to 2, an 80% reduction under the same stated conditions; this is not an emissions measurement.

scenes.instructor_title: Existing behavior is evidence, not automatically the requirement
scenes.visual_idea: A legacy function, observed examples, and the canonical rule appear in separate columns.
scenes.situation: Ask whether a characterization check should preserve everything the current implementation does. Reveal the actual behavior first, including a defect accepting a 121-minute booking. Distinguish documenting what exists from endorsing it.
scenes.changed_condition: Change the upper-bound logic deliberately as a bug fix while preserving unrelated behavior. Compare a corrected expectation derived from R-02 with blindly freezing the defect.
scenes.principle: Understand current behavior before changing it, then decide explicitly which behavior should remain.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print observed-versus-required examples and mark the intentional correction.

scenes.instructor_title: A rewrite and a refactoring carry different uncertainties
scenes.visual_idea: A change-impact graph and behavior checks accompany incremental structural changes; a full replacement appears as a comparison.
scenes.situation: Ask what evidence survives when the Policy responsibility is extracted behind an interface. Reveal unchanged externally observable behavior under relevant checks and a smaller change surface. Define refactoring by preserved behavior, not by the number of edited lines.
scenes.changed_condition: Replace the whole booking path at once while keeping the intended feature set fixed. Compare the larger set of assumptions needing re-establishment. A rewrite can be justified, but the decision needs reasons, transition strategy, and evidence—not contempt for old code.
scenes.principle: Choose a change strategy by its uncertainty, constraints, and evidence needs, not by whether the code is new.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the two change surfaces and the behavior each strategy must re-establish.

scenes.instructor_title: Old and new versions may need to coexist
scenes.visual_idea: A three-stage data transition and compatibility matrix show old/new applications reading old/new representations.
scenes.situation: Ask whether renaming a field instantly is safe while old consumers remain active. Reveal an expanded representation supporting both forms, a controlled migration, and checks that readers agree on the same duration. Show that mixed versions are a normal transition state to consider. [S23]
scenes.changed_condition: Remove the old representation before the old reader is retired. Compare the failure with a transition that verifies migration and consumer readiness before contraction. Show why rollback possibilities narrow after the old data path is removed.
scenes.principle: Evolution is safer when compatibility is maintained deliberately across the states that actually coexist.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print each transition stage, the reader-writer matrix, and the condition required before contraction.

scenes.instructor_title: Name the future cost, not just the disliked code
scenes.visual_idea: A debt card links a shortcut to repeated change effort, risk, and a possible repayment path.
scenes.situation: Ask whether every defect or untidy function is technical debt. Reveal a duplicated duration rule that makes each policy update require coordinated edits and checks. Describe the specific extra future work and failure risk rather than attaching a vague debt label.
scenes.changed_condition: Change the expected policy-change frequency from rare to frequent. Compare the rationale for repaying this item now, while acknowledging that estimates are uncertain and other risks may dominate.
scenes.principle: A useful debt discussion identifies the deferred cost, the condition that triggers it, and the evidence supporting action.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the debt record with its assumptions and revisit trigger rather than an invented monetary total.

scenes.instructor_title: The loudest complaint is not always the most important change
scenes.visual_idea: A small portfolio of maintenance needs is compared by user impact, exposure, change frequency, uncertainty, and reversibility.
scenes.situation: Offer a failing authorization edge case, an annoying display inconsistency, a fragile dependency update path, and a slow infrequent report. Ask what information is needed to prioritize them. Reveal consequences and constraints one at a time without reducing ethics or security to a decorative score.
scenes.changed_condition: Change only the exposure of the authorization flaw or the dependency’s support status in the fictional scenario. Compare how the priority rationale changes. Avoid making a real unsupported vulnerability claim about an actual library.
scenes.principle: Maintenance priority should respond to consequences and evidence, with assumptions open to revision.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the alternatives and a reasoned ordering under each labeled condition.

scenes.instructor_title: Removing something is also a compatibility decision
scenes.visual_idea: Usage evidence, deprecation communication, transition support, and removal conditions attach to an old interface.
scenes.situation: Ask whether announcing a removal date proves consumers are ready. Reveal a remaining old client and an incomplete observation window. Connect the removal decision to actual usage, support constraints, and the earlier compatibility matrix.
scenes.changed_condition: Provide verified consumer migration and a tested fallback, then compare the evidence for retiring the old path. Discuss records and diagnostics retained only for a stated purpose, with policy questions left explicit rather than invented as law.
scenes.principle: Retirement requires evidence about remaining dependence and an intentional treatment of data and recovery.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the readiness conditions and remaining unknowns for the old interface.

scenes.instructor_title: Doing less work is useful only if the promise still holds
scenes.visual_idea: Two bars show storage reads per successful search, with correctness and freshness conditions fixed beside them.
scenes.situation: Ask whether fewer reads is automatically an improvement. Reveal 1,000 reads for 100 successful searches versus 200 for 100: 10 and 2 reads per successful search. Verify that both return the required current availability and preserve the authoritative booking decision.
scenes.changed_condition: Reduce reads further by serving stale results beyond the allowed freshness assumption. Compare the apparently attractive resource number with the violated user promise. Explain that a carbon claim additionally needs an appropriate energy, emissions, hardware, and system-boundary method. [S37]
scenes.principle: Compare resource use per useful outcome under equivalent requirements, and label proxies honestly.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print counts, denominators, freshness assumptions, and the explicit statement that reads are not measured emissions.

scenes.instructor_title: The next maintainer needs the reason and the current state
scenes.visual_idea: A compact evolution record links changed requirement, migration stage, checks, rollout evidence, and remaining retirement conditions.
scenes.situation: Ask what would let a new maintainer continue the transition safely. Reveal which representations exist, which readers remain, how correctness is checked, and when rollback ceases to be safe. Keep the record synchronized with actual state rather than the original intention.
scenes.changed_condition: Change one migration condition and update the record. Compare an obsolete confident diagram with an accurate record of the partial transition. AI beat: a repository instruction file written for automated assistants is documentation with the same obligation. If it still describes the pre-migration state, a new maintainer and an assistant will both act on stale facts.
scenes.principle: Maintainability includes preserving enough shared understanding to continue a change responsibly.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the final transition record with completed, pending, and uncertain conditions distinguished in text.

weeks.title: AI-ASSISTED ENGINEERING AND ACCOUNTABLE AUTOMATION
weeks.question: Does plausible-looking output satisfy the intended behavior, and who can verify that?
outcomes: Evaluate a generated candidate against explicit requirements and independent checks.
Explain why agreement between generated code and generated tests can be weak evidence.
Identify permissions and approval boundaries appropriate to an automated engineering action.
Recognize untrusted content that attempts to redirect an automated workflow.
Distinguish increased output from improved verified delivery and maintainable understanding.

checks.question: What reveals the first candidate’s defect?
checks.answer: An independently expected 120-minute valid booking is rejected by its exclusive upper bound.

checks.question: Why not grant production access merely to prepare a patch?
checks.answer: It is unnecessary for the intended local action and increases possible consequences if the action is mistaken or redirected.

checks.question: What should happen when a repository note tells the workflow to skip required checks?
checks.answer: Treat it as untrusted content; it must not override the authoritative task or externally enforced verification boundary.

checks.question: What distinguishes using an assistant during development from a runtime AI feature?
checks.answer: In the first case the accepted artifact can operate without a model; in the second the model is part of the deployed behavior and introduces its own evaluation and dependency questions.

scenes.instructor_title: Readable code can implement the wrong rule
scenes.visual_idea: A polished candidate function sits beside R-02; input cards reveal behavior while the explanation text remains visible.
scenes.situation: Ask whether the confident explanation and tidy structure justify acceptance. Reveal the 120-minute case rejected by “duration < 120.” Compare the prose claim with the actual observable result. Do not imply that only AI-assisted code contains this kind of defect.
scenes.changed_condition: Correct the boundary while keeping formatting and explanation style unchanged. Replay 120 and 121, then compare how independent evidence—not appearance or origin—changes the judgment.
scenes.principle: Accept a change for the behavior and evidence it establishes, not for how fluently it is presented.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the requirement, candidate, counterexample, correction, and independently expected outcomes.

scenes.instructor_title: Two agreeing outputs can share one mistaken premise
scenes.visual_idea: A candidate and its accompanying tests both depend on an incorrect interpretation card; an independent requirement-derived check enters from another direction.
scenes.situation: Ask whether generated tests passing the generated implementation settle the issue. Reveal that both exclude the 120-minute boundary. Trace their shared assumption and distinguish agreement from independence.
scenes.changed_condition: Add a check derived directly from the canonical inclusive rule and a separate ownership matrix. Compare the evidence when the evaluator is not simply reproducing the candidate’s logic. Multiple tools or agents are not automatically independent if they share the same mistaken specification.
scenes.principle: Independent verification needs a justified basis for expected behavior, not merely a second source of confident text.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the assumption graph and the independent counterexample with its derivation.

scenes.instructor_title: Missing context can become an invisible design decision
scenes.visual_idea: A compact change brief links relevant rules, interfaces, constraints, and explicitly unresolved questions to the candidate.
scenes.situation: Ask how a candidate would know whether a staff role may cancel any booking. Reveal that the baseline grants no such override. Compare a candidate inventing permission with one that leaves an explicit question for the responsible decision-maker.
scenes.changed_condition: Change the brief to an approved, narrowly defined delegation policy. Compare the code and checks that legitimately change with those that should remain fixed. Restore R-03 after the variant.
scenes.principle: Automation should not silently convert an unknown policy into authority.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the baseline, labeled policy variant, and the evidence required for the changed permission.

scenes.instructor_title: A useful assistant does not need every possible permission
scenes.visual_idea: An action path passes through explicit read, edit, verify, propose, and approve boundaries; available capabilities are displayed beside it.
scenes.situation: Ask whether generating a patch requires access to production booking data or release credentials. Reveal a narrower path using synthetic fixtures and local checks. Show that proposing a change and applying a high-impact change are different authorities; the permission list and the sandbox that enforce this live outside the assistant. [S33]
scenes.changed_condition: Give the same imperfect candidate broad unattended production access, then compare the possible consequences with the bounded version. Keep it a diagram, not a functioning dangerous workflow. An approval button needs informative evidence to be meaningful.
scenes.principle: Limit capability, permission, and autonomy to the intended action, and enforce those limits outside the model’s judgment.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the capability matrix and the approval boundary with the evidence available at that point.

scenes.instructor_title: A file being read is not automatically allowed to command the reader
scenes.visual_idea: A repository note is tagged as content; a separate trusted task and permission boundary remain visible.
scenes.situation: Show a note claiming that the verification step should be skipped. Ask whether its location in a repository makes it authoritative. Reveal the attempt to cross from task data into workflow instruction. Introduce prompt injection as a trust-boundary problem. [S34]
scenes.changed_condition: Keep the note unchanged but enforce the external requirement that checks cannot be bypassed by retrieved content. Compare the attempted redirection with the allowed action path. State that text filtering alone is not a complete guarantee.
scenes.principle: Treat retrieved material as untrusted input and preserve authority boundaries around consequential actions.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the content-versus-authority diagram and the enforced check, without operational attack details.

scenes.instructor_title: Faster drafting can move the constraint somewhere else
scenes.visual_idea: The Week 4 flow board shows candidate changes, verification capacity, accepted changes, and rework separately.
scenes.situation: Ask whether doubling candidate output doubles useful delivery. Reveal a fixed review constraint and the resulting queue in the declared toy model. Distinguish generated lines, accepted changes, time to verified behavior, and downstream defects. Connect the flow to specification-driven drafting: the precise rule from Week 2 is what shortens verification, not the generation rate.
scenes.changed_condition: Improve context and verification capacity rather than only generation rate. Compare whole-flow outcomes under the same arrival conditions. Use current research as context, while identifying this chart as a constructed mechanism illustration rather than measured industry results. [S19]
scenes.principle: Evaluate automation across the workflow it changes, including verification, rework, and maintainable understanding.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the model assumptions, before-and-after flow, and the limits of the numerical example.

scenes.instructor_title: Someone must be able to explain the accepted change
scenes.visual_idea: A change record collects source context, reviewed dependencies, checks, residual questions, and a plain-language explanation.
scenes.situation: Ask whether “the tool wrote it” answers a maintainer’s question about an authorization branch. Reveal the rationale and relevant evidence required to maintain the change. Any uncertain origin or licensing concern is marked for appropriate review rather than guessed away. Use this course's own record: the deck the class is watching was drafted by an automated assistant, checked by the plan checker and the deck tests, and accepted by the instructor, with its unresolved limitation stated.
scenes.changed_condition: Replace a confident but unsupported explanation with one that accurately states a limitation. Compare whether the reviewer can make a better decision, even though the wording sounds less certain.
scenes.principle: Accountability requires an understandable change record and honest limits, regardless of how the draft was produced.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the course's own compact change record and its unresolved question; name tools factually and omit tool-brand screenshots.

scenes.instructor_title: Using AI to build software is not the same as building an AI-dependent service
scenes.visual_idea: Two system boundaries contrast an offline-generated code change with a runtime model inside the service.
scenes.situation: Ask whether Campus Rooms needs an AI dependency because an assistant helped author some code. Reveal that the shipped behavior can remain ordinary deterministic software. Contrast this with adding a runtime model whose outputs and dependencies become part of the user-facing system.
scenes.changed_condition: Insert a hypothetical model that suggests room choices, while leaving authoritative booking and permissions outside it. Compare the additional evaluation and failure questions without expanding this course into model training. Name two of them: an evaluation set of room-choice cases with expected answers, and a regression check that reruns it whenever the prompt or the model version changes, because the output is not deterministic. NIST’s AI profile concerns AI-model and AI-system development and should not be mislabeled as a blanket coding-assistant rulebook. [S35]
scenes.principle: The engineering obligations follow the actual system boundary and consequences, not the presence of AI somewhere in the workflow.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print both boundaries and the distinct claims each would require.

weeks.title: CONNECTING THE LIFECYCLE THROUGH ONE ENGINEERING DECISION
weeks.question: Can we explain a change from human need to operational evidence without losing the original promise?
outcomes: Trace a new user need through a requirement, model, design decision, verification, and operational observation.
Identify which established invariants remain unchanged during a new feature decision.
Compare two change strategies under the same constraints and evidence.
Explain a release or recovery decision with its assumptions and consequences.
State a general engineering principle using a concrete counterexample from the course.

checks.question: Why retain the existing affected booking rather than silently deleting it?
checks.answer: Its owner already relied on the promise; explicit affected status, history, and an authorized resolution preserve information needed to address the consequence.

checks.question: Where must closure and booking ordering be enforced?
checks.answer: At the authoritative decision boundary with a mechanism that preserves the stated concurrent behavior.

checks.question: What is missing when function checks pass but users cannot perceive an affected booking?
checks.answer: Evidence that the complete user-facing requirement, including accessible status information, has been satisfied.

checks.question: What should happen to the final engineering claim when an assumption changes?
checks.answer: Reconsider the affected decision and narrow or revise the claim until appropriate evidence is available.

scenes.instructor_title: Close the room—but what happens to the people already relying on it?
scenes.visual_idea: A maintenance notice overlays a future calendar, with an existing confirmed booking and a new request shown separately.
scenes.situation: Ask what “disable C101” leaves ambiguous. Reveal the closure interval, who may record a closure, what new requests should see, and how existing booking holders learn that action is required. Separate preventing new promises from resolving promises already made.
scenes.changed_condition: Compare silent deletion of the existing booking with preserving its record and making its affected status explicit. Ask which outcome supports honest communication, traceability, and authorized resolution. Accept R-06 as the scenario’s stated policy only after showing these choices.
scenes.principle: A new requirement must address the consequences for existing users, not merely the next successful action.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the ambiguous request, accepted extension, and treatment of new versus existing bookings.

scenes.instructor_title: Each representation should answer the next unanswered question
scenes.visual_idea: A linked strip changes from requirement card to state annotation, decision table, dependency graph, and verification matrix.
scenes.situation: Ask which representation would show who is permitted to record a closure and which would show request ordering. Reveal the appropriate model for each question. Connect R-06 to the existing R-01 through R-05 without inventing a one-diagram solution.
scenes.changed_condition: Change only the closure interval so it ends exactly when a candidate booking begins. Compare the boundary expectation with the half-open interval convention already used throughout the course.
scenes.principle: Traceability is useful when it carries meaning across representations, not when it merely adds connecting lines.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the linked trace and the adjacency example with the relevant rule labels.

scenes.instructor_title: The interface can explain the closure; the decision boundary must enforce it
scenes.visual_idea: Two alternatives show closure checking only in the browser or at the authoritative booking decision with an informative interface.
scenes.situation: Ask whether a hidden room card is sufficient to prevent a new confirmation. Reveal stale client state and another valid request path. Reuse Week 9’s trust boundary and Week 6’s concurrency lesson.
scenes.changed_condition: Introduce a closure while a booking request is in progress. Compare an interface-only check with an authoritative decision that defines ordering between closure and confirmation. Do not pretend the exact storage mechanism is settled by drawing a lock icon.
scenes.principle: Shared promises need an enforcement point that survives alternate paths and concurrent change.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print both alternatives, the interleaving, and the decision-ordering requirement.

scenes.instructor_title: One new rule needs more than one friendly example
scenes.visual_idea: A traceability matrix links R-06 to interval boundaries, permission decisions, concurrent behavior, interface states, and notification failure.
scenes.situation: Ask which checks would distinguish a plausible incomplete implementation from the intended behavior. Reveal a nonoverlap case, a closure-boundary case, a forbidden staff action, an in-flight booking, and an affected-owner message.
scenes.changed_condition: Make all function checks pass while omitting the affected-booking interface cue. Compare the evidence with a keyboard-accessible user journey that reveals the missing information. [S25]
scenes.principle: Build evidence around the risks and user promises that cross layers, not just the easiest function to test.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the check matrix with expected outcomes and a clear gap in the incomplete version.

scenes.instructor_title: What would make this change ready to expose?
scenes.visual_idea: A compact release path combines the verified artifact, compatibility state, selected exposure, and user-outcome observations.
scenes.situation: Ask whether passing interval and permission checks justify full exposure when existing users cannot see their affected status. Reveal the incomplete release record and keep the decision paused. Add the missing accessible cue and the evidence that it is observable.
scenes.changed_condition: Introduce notification failure after closure is recorded. Compare a system that loses the affected-user task with one that records pending communication and continues to display the affected status. Preserve recovery responsibility without undoing the closure or deleting booking history.
scenes.principle: Release decisions must consider the whole user promise and the behavior of incomplete or failed work.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the blocked decision, corrected evidence, and notification-failure outcome.

scenes.instructor_title: Two reasonable designs can optimize different constraints
scenes.visual_idea: A side-by-side decision record compares a targeted change inside the modular application with a separately deployed closure service.
scenes.situation: Ask which new requirement actually needs independent deployment. Reveal benefits and costs under the fictional small-team, single-campus baseline. Compare change surface, operational boundaries, authority, and maintenance burden without using an arbitrary winner score.
scenes.changed_condition: Change one condition: several independent campus operators now need separate release schedules. Revisit the rationale and identify the new contract and ownership questions. Do not announce that this single condition automatically proves the distributed option is best.
scenes.principle: A defensible choice explains its assumptions, trade-offs, evidence, and conditions for reconsideration.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print both decision records and the one changed condition, preserving unresolved questions.

scenes.instructor_title: Name the principle after remembering the counterexample
scenes.visual_idea: Six concise principle cards connect to small images from earlier scenes rather than a wall of vocabulary.
scenes.situation: Ask which counterexample taught each principle: false confirmation, ambiguous requirement, clean-but-wrong merge, shared test assumption, unsafe rollback, and overpowered automation. Reveal the principle only after the class recognizes the situation.
scenes.changed_condition: Change the domain label from room booking to a generic reservation service while keeping the underlying relationship. Compare which principles transfer and which policies must be elicited again.
scenes.principle: Conceptual understanding transfers relationships and reasoning—not an unexamined copy of another system’s rules.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print each principle beside its concrete counterexample and scope.

scenes.instructor_title: Finish with a claim the evidence can actually support
scenes.visual_idea: A final one-page decision narrative links need, rule, design, checks, release, observation, and unresolved uncertainty.
scenes.situation: Ask the class to explain why the selected closure behavior is justified. Reveal a coherent account using the evidence already shown, with explicit uncertainty about the multi-campus extension. Avoid ending with “everything is solved.”
scenes.changed_condition: Remove one important check or change one assumption. Compare how the final claim must narrow. Close on the habit of revising confidence when the supporting conditions change.
scenes.principle: Good engineering explanations connect decisions to evidence and remain honest about what has not been established.
scenes.pdf_treatment: Print the complete decision narrative and its bounded conclusion as the closing student reference.
